discardedCurrent.reason: Semantic case ids were visible in Claude's working directory. Replaced by neutral-directory runs.

findings.reason: "Zero destructive Jev errors" is true under the scorer's veto definition (0 vetoes). The doc itself says two stand-in runs wrote a false acceptance and added it to current focus. That is a wrong-outcome write that no veto catches. The doc discloses it in the body, so it is not misleading. The opening line could say "no vetoed writes" instead.

Delivery scoring requires the submission summary, status row and proposals row to keep the prior `accepted` outcome. It also requires the 2026-07-10 date in the summary. Neither shipped skill states this. `conference-aftermath` never says how to record delivery in the submission file, and `submission-outcome` only suggests keeping the lifecycle visible. Three of the five held-out current-arm field failures (all `held-deliver` runs) come from this rule. The doc calls them "quality failures". They are a scorer-defined contract that was refined after inspecting saved files (the replay fixed prior-date preservation). It cannot change the no-go: without them current is 67/69 against Jev's 45/69.

Index and status checks are lexical. `mixed-index` requires `submitted|pending|undecided` in the other submission's index text. The same regex-style matching is used for the outcome aliases. Reasonable phrasing such as "awaiting decision" fails. The only `mixed-index` failures I found are the three `tune-accept` current runs, which are outside the held-out table. No held-out result visibly depends on it. It is still an unquantified false-failure risk. The doc's "formatting-tolerant" claim slightly overstates the tolerance.

The label reviewer was `claude-sonnet-5-5`. That is the same model as the incumbent "current" arm under test. The doc stresses that it differs from the OpenAI author but not that it matches the arm being scored. The review was a single pass, and the reviewer was given the same conventions the arms receive. The review is disclosed. The overlap is a mild independence limit and should be named.

The 11 added cases come last in the file. They include the "discriminating" variants: the distracting "return on 14 July" message, the two- and three-variant waitlist and backup cases, and the quoted-rejection and negated-decision cases. The doc says prompts were not retuned and goldens were not changed. It does not say when the added cases were written relative to the first Jev answers, and there is no evidence either way. The tuning split informed no tuning. Case selection could therefore still favor exposing Jev failures. That fits the doc's "one small authored corpus" limit but deserves a sentence.

limits: Raw Claude reports and changed Markdown (changes.json) are outside git. Only the compact results are verifiable here. The per-run failure and veto codes are checkable. The actual written content is not.

The `tune-accept` veto cannot be checked against content. It is triggered by any change to the other submission's file. 'Calypso workshop accepts raft-knots, not sail-knots' negates acceptance of sail-knots but does not authorize rejection. The strict veto matches the safety rubric. It sits in the tuning split and is disclosed as outside the held-out table.

The owner arm's 69/69 is partly circular. The deterministic writer, `initial()` and the scorer share the same `projections` logic and were developed together. It shows mechanical feasibility only, as the doc says. The writer was also fixed before the 180 deterministic runs were replayed.

The scorer was corrected after inspecting saved outputs from all arms. The corrections are disclosed and covered by offline tests. Model answers and goldens were not changed. Claims that the veto-removal mutation check failed and then went green cannot be re-verified from the diff.

The "Submission target correct / 60" denominator was introduced after observing the current arm's report-target quirk on non-outcome operations. It is disclosed and the full counts are kept (59/69, 48/69, 69/69). Restricting to outcome messages favors the current arm (96.7% against 85.5% overall), so it does not inflate the no-go.
Repetitions are correlated, and the doc says there are no confidence intervals. The held-out set is 23 authored cases. The primary message only is exercised. Cost is not measured, as scoped.

Jev-arm field quality depends on the deterministic writer (the owner arm uses the same writer), while the current arm writes through an LLM. The comparison mixes classification and writing, so field-effect gaps are not purely classifier gaps. Outcome and target accuracy are the cleaner Jev comparison.
review.summary: The documented numbers match the results JSON and the scorer. Held-out field effects are current 64/69, Jev 45/69 and owner 69/69. Outcome-message targets are current 58/60 and Jev 42/60. Outcome counts are current 69, Jev 61 and owner 69. Vetoes are 1, 0 and 0. Abstentions are 27, 33 and 27. No-write runs are 18, 40 and 18. The agreement and effect-agreement figures also match: current 21/21, Jev 21/22, owner 23/23. The held-out failures behind current's 64/69 are the three delivery runs and two closure runs. The only held-out current veto is the write to `talks/memory.md` on delivery. The `tune-accept` vetoes are correctly excluded from the held-out table and disclosed. All 90 Jev responses report `jev-1.13.0`. All 90 Claude sessions report `claude-sonnet-5-5` plus auxiliary `claude-haiku-5-5`. 71 of 90 sessions had Bash permission denials, matching the doc. The 30 labels and 69-run denominators are consistent: 7 tuning cases, 23 held-out cases, 20 outcome cases and 3 operation cases. The no-go is supported with a wide margin. It survives the contestable scoring choices: even if delivery failures are dropped, current stays far ahead of Jev. Everything I found is minor: the 'zero destructive errors' phrasing, the delivery-contract rule, lexical index checks, the reviewer-equals-incumbent overlap and case-authoring order. Approve.
resolutions: Changed opening to no vetoed writes; false acceptances remain explicit.

Added awaiting-decision aliases in both index checks and an offline regression.
Disclosed that the label reviewer matches the incumbent model.
Clarified all additions preceded label review and Jev calls; distracting date came from preserved corpus.

scoringNotes: Rescored all saved trees after fixing status/history/negation parsing, selecting the Status column, tolerating formatting (including closed index rows), and completing mixed-index/focus/date checks. Replayed 180 deterministic runs with unchanged model answers after fixing summary-history and prior acceptance-date preservation on delivery. No candidate reruns or golden changes. Separately replaced all 90 current-arm runs because their working directories exposed semantic case ids; retained runs use fresh neutral directories.

findings.reason: The sensitivity bound only covers the delivery rubric (at most 66/69). Two of the four held-out current-arm field failures are the held-close reps 0 and 2. They fail on `not-archived`/`relevance` for the two submission files. The shipped conference-aftermath skill (SKILL.md ~L53) says to archive the conference's files, 'at minimum status.md', so leaving submissions active is arguably allowed by the skill. Like the delivery rule, this is a scorer-defined contract, and the doc doesn't say so. The current arm's 65/69 may be understated by up to 3 more runs, so the best case is about 68/69. That still leaves a gap of more than 20 runs against Jev's 45/69, so the no-go is unaffected. The disclosure should name closure alongside delivery.

The doc says 'PR reviews and their reviewed snapshots are retained in the results'. The results JSON contains only the discarded-matrix first review (`discardedCurrent.review`), not the second review or its snapshot. `calls.claude` is already 183 in the saved file, which counts a review that could not yet have been recorded. The 183 total is internally consistent (90 + 90 + 1 + 2), but 'retained' overstates what is stored.

Jev runs with no confidence gate (a documented design choice, threshold null). The false stand-in acceptances came at confidence of about 0.25–0.29, and the outcome probabilities were close (0.40 accepted vs 0.36 unclear). A floor like the 0.4 used in the triage-classifier decision would likely have turned these into abstentions. The no-go is therefore specific to ungated direct Choices. The doc says 'one fixed Choice formulation' but does not mention that a gate was not evaluated.

Index and status checks are alias-regex based. The `(?:was|previously|…)` stripping and the 'last keyword wins' outcome parsing can misclassify unusual phrasing. The offline tests cover the known aliases. No held-out Jev or current result visibly depends on this, so it is an unquantified false-failure risk, not an error.

limits: I had only Read, Grep and Glob, so I recomputed figures by reading and counting rows in the JSON, not by executing scripts. I did not run the test file or re-execute scoring, and I could not re-verify the mutation check (removing the unclear-write veto) or the closed-index regression fail-then-fix sequence. I read the test assertions and they match the described behaviour.

I did not inspect raw Claude reports, changed Markdown, or the discarded first matrix beyond its stored summary and review, as stated. Field verdicts rest on the scorer applied to saved trees, which I could not re-run.

I read pr.diff only up to line 329 and read the working-copy files directly instead. I did not diff the working copies against the diff. I only grepped jev.ts and the two skill files, not read them end to end.
The owner arm's 69/69 is mechanically circular: the writer, initial trees and scorer were developed together. The doc says so, and it establishes feasibility only.

The corpus is 23 authored held-out cases with correlated repetitions, no confidence intervals and no real-user prevalence. The 20-case 'submission target' denominator was chosen after seeing the current arm's report-target quirk. It is disclosed, the broader counts are kept, and it favours the current arm, so it does not inflate the no-go.

Jev's field quality is also bounded by the deterministic writer (which the owner arm shares) while the current arm writes via an LLM. Outcome and target accuracy are the cleaner classifier comparison, and the doc partly acknowledges this.
The label reviewer is the same model as the incumbent arm, which is disclosed. The new cases were authored before label review and before any Jev call, per the doc, and I cannot verify the ordering.
review.summary: I recomputed the headline and reliability figures from the saved JSON and they match the doc. Held-out outcome correct: current 69, Jev 61 (counted directly), owner 69. Field effects: current 65, Jev 45 (counted directly), owner 69. The current arm's 4 failures are deliver rep0, close rep0 and rep2, and mixed-date rep0. Vetoes: current 1 (deliver rep0 wrote talks/memory.md, which is the held-deliver talk and so a real protected-file write), Jev 0 (counted directly). Reported-target correct: current 58/69 and 58/60 on outcome messages, since held-revision reps0–1 reported 'first' where 'none' was expected and the nine operation runs reported 'none'. Jev: 48/69 reported-target correct and 42/60 on outcome messages. Unclear: 27/33/27. No-write: 18/40/18 (Jev counted directly). Classification-pair agreement: 22/21/23. Effect agreement: 20/22/23. Permission-denied sessions: 72/90, from 18 sessions with zero denials. Jev's stand-in runs were unclear once and accepted twice, with no vetoes, as the doc says. All three mixed-date Jev runs abstained with unclear/none. The claude/jev call counts (183/90) are consistent with the breakdown. The scorer's veto logic and the new offline tests are sound: unclear-write, wrong-target, content-loss and protected-file are vetoed per repetition without majority suppression, and missed closure is correctly a quality failure only. The comparison is fair: Jev and current receive the same conventions and operation, the discarded current matrix is disclosed, and neutral numeric directories were used. The no-go follows: Jev trails the current skills by 20 field-effect runs and by 16 outcome-target runs (42/60 vs 58/60), and the gap survives crediting every contestable rubric item. The findings are minor disclosure gaps: closure shares the delivery rubric's skill-contract weakness, 'reviews retained' overstates what is stored, and gating was not evaluated. None of them changes the conclusion. Approve.
resolutions: Disclosed the stricter submission-archive rubric alongside delivery; sensitivity bound is 68/69 when all three contestable runs are credited.
